title: Ecommerce development

seo.title: Ecommerce website development
seo.description: Ecommerce development on Shopify, WooCommerce or custom Next.js, with B2B pricing, quoting and ERP integration. Fixed-price builds from $12,000.

answerBlock: Ecommerce development is designing and building an online store, from the catalogue and checkout to the pricing rules and systems behind it. Calwebtech builds on Shopify, WooCommerce or a custom Next.js storefront, including B2B account pricing, quoting and ERP integration. Most stores cost between $12,000 and $60,000, depending mainly on catalogue size and integrations.

hero.outcome: A store where buyers find the right product quickly, see the right price for their account, and send orders straight into the systems you already run.

problem.heading: When does a business need ecommerce development rather than a theme?
problem.intro: Ecommerce projects usually begin when the store stops matching how the business actually sells.

situations.title: Trade buyers still phone or email orders
situations.body: Your prices depend on the account, so the website shows a contact form and your team retypes every order into the ERP.

situations.title: The catalogue is too big to browse
situations.body: Thousands of products, variants or parts make search and filtering the whole experience, and the theme's search was not built for that.

situations.title: Checkout loses people at the last step
situations.body: Traffic and add-to-cart look healthy, but buyers leave during checkout and nobody can say exactly where or why.

included.heading: What does an ecommerce build include?
included.intro: Every build is scoped around your catalogue, your pricing rules and the systems orders need to reach.
items: A written platform recommendation: Shopify, WooCommerce or a custom Next.js storefront
Catalogue structure, a product data model and faceted search and filtering
Account-specific pricing, tiered terms and customer groups for B2B buyers
Quote requests and quote-to-order flows alongside standard checkout
Catalogue and inventory sync with your ERP or inventory system
Checkout tuned against real drop-off, with the payment methods your buyers use
Product configurators for made-to-order items where you need them
Order, shipping and tax rules set up and tested against real scenarios
Technical SEO for product and category pages, with redirects from any old store
A written performance budget for product and category pages on mobile
Training for your team on products, orders and promotions

process.heading: How does an ecommerce project run?
process.intro: Nine weeks is typical for a store with integrations. A focused store without them is closer to six to eight.

steps.title: Discovery
steps.body: Catalogue, pricing rules, fulfilment and the systems orders must reach. The platform decision and a fixed scope come out of this week.

steps.title: Design
steps.body: Category, search, product, cart and checkout screens designed for how your buyers actually shop, on a phone as well as a desk.

steps.title: Build and integrate
steps.body: Storefront, product data, pricing rules and integrations built on staging, with test orders run through your own systems.

steps.title: Prove
steps.body: End-to-end order testing, payment and tax checks, accessibility and performance passes, and redirects from the old store.

steps.title: Launch and tune
steps.body: Cutover, monitoring and team training, then a first look at checkout drop-off once real orders arrive.

technology.heading: Which ecommerce platforms and technologies do you use?
technology.intro: The platform follows your catalogue, pricing rules and team, not our preference.

pricing.heading: How much does an ecommerce website cost?
pricing.intro: Most stores land between $12,000 and $60,000. A focused store on Shopify or WooCommerce sits at the lower end; account pricing, quoting and ERP integration move it towards the top.

factors.title: Catalogue size and data quality
factors.body: A few hundred clean products import quickly. Tens of thousands of parts with messy attributes need cleaning and a data model before search can work.

factors.title: Pricing rules
factors.body: Retail pricing is simple. Account-specific prices, tiers, contract terms and quote-to-order flows add design, build and testing.

factors.title: Integrations
factors.body: ERP, inventory, shipping and accounting connections are usually the largest single cost, and older systems take longer.

factors.title: Configurators
factors.body: Made-to-order products with options, dependencies and live pricing need their own interface and rules.

factors.title: Platform
factors.body: Shopify and WooCommerce cover standard stores for less. A custom Next.js storefront costs more and pays off when the rules are unusual.

faq.heading: What do buyers ask before an ecommerce build?

items.question: Should we use Shopify, WooCommerce or a custom build?
items.answer: Shopify suits most direct-to-consumer stores that want hosting and payments handled for them. WooCommerce suits teams already on WordPress who want control of their data. A custom Next.js storefront makes sense when pricing rules, catalogue size or integrations push past what either handles well. We recommend one in writing before you commit.

items.question: Can the store show different prices to different trade accounts?
items.answer: Yes. Account-specific pricing, tiered terms and customer groups are a core part of our B2B builds, so a signed-in buyer sees their own prices and can order or request a quote without calling.

items.question: Can the store connect to our ERP?
items.answer: Usually. We sync catalogue, inventory and orders both ways so your team stops retyping. The first step is checking what your ERP exposes, which happens before the proposal so the price reflects the real work.

items.question: How long does an ecommerce build take?
items.answer: Six to eight weeks for a focused store without integrations, and nine to fourteen weeks when account pricing, configurators or ERP integration are involved.

items.question: Will we lose search traffic when we move platforms?
items.answer: Not if the migration is done properly. We map every product, category and page URL to its new address with permanent redirects before launch, and monitor Search Console for the first thirty days.

items.question: Can you migrate our existing products and customers?
items.answer: Yes. Products, categories, customers and order history can move, with the data cleaned and matched rather than copied as it is. Passwords usually cannot move between platforms, so we plan how returning customers set a new one.

items.question: Who owns the store when it is finished?
items.answer: You do, completely. The repository, the database, the design files and every third party account are registered in your name and transferred at handover. There is no proprietary format and no vendor holding your data.
